article.title: How AI could ‘supercharge’ election risks across south-east Asia
article.full_text: Years ago it would have been an elaborate operation involving an army of cyber troops creating fake news websites, social media accounts and forged dossiers, all deployed to spread disinformation en masse. Now, all you need is AI. In a worrying sign of how AI could “supercharge” fake news, Anthropic recently revealed how Claude AI was used in a political influence operation in Malaysia. It created a commercial election manipulation platform, utilising a network of about 1,000 X accounts, a fake news outlet called “Malaysia Pulse” and a series of fabricated documents. The operation appeared designed to target voters in recent state elections, pulling in census and electoral data to exploit sensitive political and social fractures, including race, religion, and royalty across all 222 Malaysian parliamentary constituencies. The experiment was ultimately ineffective once Anthropic stepped in but has sparked alarm about how AI could be weaponised in future elections in south-east Asia, a region already deeply vulnerable to fake news. Katie Harbath, who formerly worked on public policy for global elections at Meta, says the case is an example of how AI brings a new level of sophistication and ease to the disinformation landscape. “AI can supercharge it in terms of you can make a lot more content that’s more personalised, quicker and cheaper,” says Harbath, who now heads the tech consultancy company Anchor Change. “But you still need a distribution mechanism, and at the moment, that’s still your more social media type platforms.” Anthropic detailed the Malaysia election operation in its latest threat assessment, released in September. The report revealed how actors used Claude to build networks of fake social media profiles and news websites that targeted audiences on six continents. Anthropic said the actors included “governments, state-aligned propaganda institutions and state media, as well as private firms selling influence”. ‘Flood the zone’ South-east Asia is no stranger to disinformation. In recent years Nobel laureate and Filipino journalist Maria Ressa has likened the Philippines to a “petri dish” for the weaponisation of disinformation and fake news, with techniques tried and tested in the south-east Asian nation later successfully replicated in the west. But AI makes it all much easier. “Basically AI is just mimicking what we would have, I guess, termed a few years ago, a troll factory,” says Rossine Fallorina of Sigla, a Philippine thinktank that researches AI. “Mostly because it speeds up the production process. So you don’t need 10 people to create a narrative or a story. You can just prompt it and then have it propagated.” Last year OpenAI banned accounts using AI to generate comments about Philippine politics and public officials across social platforms, with many fictitious comments generated in support of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr. Across south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper connected populations, some fear the divisive potential of AI on social media. “It feeds political polarisation and it feeds on divisions,” says Bridget Welsh, from the University of Nottingham Asia Research Institute Malaysia. “That’s really what’s concerning about the fragmented nature of what’s happening in Malaysia.” Malaysia’s general election could be called for late 2027, while the Philippines and Cambodia have polls in 2028, and Indonesia the following year. Already in the region, AI has been effective. In Indonesia, an AI-generated cartoon image of now-president Prabowo Subianto that helped soften his strongman image became wildly popular in the 2024 election. It has also been used to inflame tensions, such as inciting hatred toward ethnic Rohingya refugees who fled to Malaysia from Myanmar during the civil war, says Dr Ben Loh, a media lecturer at Monash University Malaysia. “It’s come to the point where people already have this deep-seated hate in their minds and when they see the content like this,

article.title: AI is getting more powerful, but safeguards aren't keeping up
‘Self-healing’ coach who was banned from working in Australia to speak in UK
article.full_text: A controversial proponent of natural remedies who has been banned from providing any health services in Australia is due to embark on a series of events in the UK and Ireland despite criticism from scientists, health charities and academic bodies. Barbara O’Neill, who describes herself as a naturopath and nutritionist, lectures internationally on “natural self-healing”. She has previously claimed that cancer is a fungus that can be treated with bicarbonate soda, that vaccines have caused an epidemic of conditions including autism and cot death, and that pregnant women with Strep B do not have to take antibiotics. Now experts in the UK have raised concerns in a letter to venues across UK and Ireland where O’Neill, 73, is scheduled to speak. The letter – which was organised by Dr David Robert Grimes, a science communicator and expert in Biostatistics at Trinity College Dublin – describes O’Neill as “a leading vector of medical misinformation”, adding that she repeatedly made “misguided medical assertions”, gave “unqualified advice” and promoted “abject demonisation of conventional medical treatment.” The letter notes that O’Neill charges thousands of dollars for retreats and telephone consultations, and raises concerns about the events due to be held at the venues. “At the event, she will spread dangerous health fictions to a susceptible audience, leeching off an illusion of legitimacy afforded to her by the surrounds of your respectable establishment,” it said. Among those who have signed the letter are Orla Dolan, the chief executive of Breakthrough Cancer Research; Prof Colin Doherty, head of Trinity College Dublin School of Medicine; Prof David Colquhoun, a fellow of the Royal Society and University College London; and Sander van der Linden, professor of Psychology at the University of Cambridge. Grimes, who has authored a book on medical misinformation, told the Guardian that O’Neill presented as a kindly grandmother dispensing natural wisdom. “Medical misinformation kills, and we wrote the letter because we have seen first-hand the profound and tragic harms that health fictions inflict on vulnerable patients … We hope making people aware of this reality mitigates her ability to inflict harm elsewhere,” he said. According to recent findings by the UK’s Academy of Medical Sciences, 67% of UK adults see health misinformation as a significant or very serious problem, with 89% viewing it as putting lives at risk. O’Neill is no stranger to controversy. In 2019, the New South Wales Health Care Complaints Commission (HCCC) in Australia concluded an investigation into her professional conduct. Among its findings, the investigation found O’Neill “does not recognise that she is misleading vulnerable people (including mothers and cancer sufferers) by providing very selective information. The misinformation has real potential to have a detrimental effect on the health of individuals because Mrs O’Neill also discourages mainstream treatment for cancer, antibiotics and vaccinations.” She was permanently barred from providing any health services either voluntarily or in a paid capacity. The HCCC has confirmed its prohibition orders are enforceable across all of Australia. However, the ruling has not prevented O’Neill and her husband, Michael, from running events in other countries, including the UK, where she has given seminars at the luxury golf resort Trump Turnberry among other venues. The latest string of engagements includes a five-day retreat at the Cranage Estate in Cheshire in early October. Titled A Taste of Misty Mountain, the event includes lectures by O’Neill with titles such as What Really Does Cause Disease, The Science of Breath and The Immune System, as well as talks by Michael, including one titled Barbara Under Attack. A ticket for the event, which includes a dinner dance, costs £700.
